title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Vegetation — 2024
subject: biology
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Describe the major vegetation zones of Nepal according to altitude.
questions.solution: **Tropical (<1000 m):** sal (*Shorea robusta*), simal. **Sub-tropical (1000–2000 m):** chir pine, alder. **Temperate (2000–3000 m):** oak, rhododendron. **Sub-alpine (3000–4000 m):** fir, birch, juniper. **Alpine (>4000 m):** meadows, cushion plants; **nival:** permanent snow, no vegetation.
questions.knowledgeNote: Nepal compresses tropics-to-tundra into 200 km — the world's steepest vegetation staircase.
questions.answer: **Major vegetation zones of Nepal by altitude (bottom to top):** **(1) Tropical (Terai, ~70–500 m)** — sal (*Shorea robusta*) tropical deciduous forest and tall riverine grasslands; **(2) Subtropical (~500–2000 m)** — chir pine (*Pinus roxburghii*) on dry slopes and schima–castanopsis broad-leaved forest on moist slopes; **(3) Temperate (~2000–3000 m)** — oak–rhododendron forest and temperate conifers (blue pine, fir, spruce); **(4) Sub-alpine (~3000–4000 m)** — birch (*Betula utilis*)–rhododendron scrub, juniper; tree line ≈ 4000 m; **(5) Alpine (~4000–5000 m)** — alpine meadows, cushion plants, dwarf shrubs; **(6) Nival (> 5000 m)** — snow and ice with only lichens and mosses. **Deep point:** the ladder is a thermometer — temperature falls ~6 °C per 1000 m, and each vegetation belt is simply the plant community that tolerates that band.

questions.question: Distinguish between tropical deciduous and temperate evergreen forests of Nepal.
questions.solution:
**Tropical deciduous** (Terai–Siwalik, <1000 m): shed leaves in dry summer (sal, simal); hot monsoon climate.

**Temperate evergreen** (Mahabharat–mid-hills, 2000–3000 m): retain leaves year-round (oak, rhododendron, pines); cool with winter frost.
questions.knowledgeNote: Deciduousness dodges drought; evergreenness endures cold — leaf habit maps directly onto climate stress.
questions.answer: **Tropical deciduous forest (Terai, < 500 m):** dominated by **sal (*Shorea robusta*)** with sissau, khair, semal; hot climate, monsoon-deciduous (many species shed leaves in the dry season); tall dense forest, rich in teak-like hardwoods; associated with one-horned rhino, tiger, swamp deer habitat. **Temperate evergreen forest (2000–3000 m):** dominated by **oaks (*Quercus* spp.) and rhododendrons** with laurels and magnolias; cool climate; leaves broad and evergreen (replaced gradually, not all shed at once); mosses, ferns and orchids abundant on trunks; mixed broad-leaved stands on moist slopes, merging with conifers higher up. **Differences:** altitude/climate (hot monsoon vs cool temperate); dominants (sal vs oak–rhododendron); leaf-shedding pattern (dry-season deciduous vs evergreen); associated fauna and undergrowth. **Deep point:** 'deciduous vs evergreen' is a water strategy, not a climate badge — the Terai forest drops its leaves to survive the dry *season*, the temperate forest keeps its leaves because its climate never dries hard enough to force the gamble.

questions.question: In which vegetation zone is sal (*Shorea robusta*) dominant? Write two of its economic uses.
questions.solution:
**Tropical zone** (Terai and Siwalik, below ~1000 m) — sal forms nearly pure stands.

**Uses:** premier construction timber (houses, sleepers) and leaves as traditional plates (duna-tapari) plus religious offerings.
questions.knowledgeNote: Sal's resinous durability made it the Terai's timber backbone — and the centre of community-forestry conflicts.
questions.answer: **Zone:** sal is the dominant species of the **tropical deciduous forest zone (Terai, ~70–500 m)** — the flagship timber forest of the Nepalese lowlands. **Two economic uses:** (1) **timber** — hard, durable, termite-resistant construction wood (houses, railway sleepers, furniture, doors); (2) **resin/tannin and other products** — sal resin (dhuna) and seeds (for oil) are harvested; the leaves are used for plates (tapari) and fodder. **Deep point:** sal's worth is its wood chemistry — dense, resin-rich, rot-resistant; it is the reason the Terai forests were heavily logged and why their conservation now matters commercially as well as ecologically.

questions.question: What are the major causes of deforestation in Nepal?
questions.solution: Fuel-wood dependence, agricultural expansion and resettlement, illegal logging and smuggling, infrastructure (roads, dams), forest fires, and overgrazing.
questions.knowledgeNote: Community forestry reversed the 1980s crisis in the hills — the Terai frontier remains the pressure point.
questions.answer: **Major causes of deforestation in Nepal:** (1) **expanding agriculture and shifting cultivation** — forest cleared for farmland and grazing as population grows; (2) **firewood and timber extraction** — over 70% of Nepal's energy still comes from burning wood; illegal logging; (3) **infrastructure and urbanisation** — roads, settlements, quarries consuming forest land; (4) **forest fires and overgrazing** — annual dry-season fires and uncontrolled livestock preventing regeneration. **Deep point:** the drivers are demand-side — population, fuel and food pressure — which is why purely punitive conservation fails and community stewardship (community forestry) succeeded.

questions.question: What is community forestry? Explain its role in vegetation conservation in Nepal.
questions.solution:
**Community forestry** hands state forests to local user groups who protect, harvest sustainably, and share benefits.

It reversed hill deforestation: user groups patrol, replant, and regulate grazing — forest cover in programme areas has measurably regenerated while funding schools and trails.
questions.knowledgeNote: Nepal's programme is a global model — devolution succeeding where central policing failed.
questions.answer: **Community forestry:** a programme (begun nationally with the **Forest Act 1993**, building on the 1970s–80s pilots) in which the government **hands over a defined patch of national forest to a local Community Forest User Group (CFUG)** — the community gets the right to manage, harvest and sell forest products, in return for the duty to protect and regenerate the forest under an approved operational plan. **Role in vegetation conservation:** (1) **reversal of degradation** — Nepal's forest cover has measurably recovered under community management (from ~40% of Terai/hill forests degraded in the 1980s to net regrowth); (2) **local ownership ends open-access abuse** — users who guard the forest gain from it (firewood, fodder, leaf litter on a sustainable quota); (3) **income and reinvestment** — CFUG funds build schools, trails and plantations; (4) **biodiversity and springs protection** — community forests shelter wildlife and protect watersheds. Nepal's community forestry is a world-recognised model. **Deep point:** the programme's insight is tenure — people deforest what no one owns and protect what they do; making villagers the forest's shareholders did what policing alone never could.

questions.question: Distinguish between in-situ and ex-situ conservation with one Nepalese example of each.
questions.solution:
**In-situ:** protecting species in natural habitat — e.g. Chitwan National Park (rhino, tiger).

**Ex-situ:** protecting outside habitat — e.g. Central Zoo, Lalitpur, or the Godavari botanical garden seed banks.

In-situ preserves evolution in place; ex-situ is the backup for the critically endangered.
questions.knowledgeNote: 12 national parks + reserves + conservation areas form Nepal's in-situ network — pair the concept with the map.
questions.answer: **In-situ conservation:** protecting species **in their natural habitat** — the organism stays where it lives and evolves. **Nepalese examples:** **national parks and reserves** — e.g. **Chitwan National Park** (one-horned rhino, Bengal tiger), Sagarmatha NP, Shey-Phoksundo NP; community forests; protected areas covering ~23% of Nepal. **Ex-situ conservation:** protecting species **outside their natural habitat** — in collections, stores or laboratories. **Nepalese examples:** **Central Zoo, Jawalakhel** (conservation breeding); **National Herbarium and Botanical Gardens (Godawari/Lalitpur)** preserving plant specimens and living collections; seed banks and tissue-culture labs (e.g. for orchids and crop wild relatives). **Differences:** in-situ conserves whole ecosystems and ongoing evolution but is exposed to habitat pressures; ex-situ is a last-resort insurance for critically endangered species, cheap to study but evolutionarily frozen and expensive to maintain. **Deep point:** in-situ saves the *library*, ex-situ saves *photocopies of single books* — the ideal strategy is in-situ first, ex-situ as the backup for species whose habitat cannot be saved in time.
